facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: On the reported basis, Hilton Grand Vacations carries corporate debt of 4,946 (gross) at September 30, 2026 against LTM Adjusted EBITDA of 1,434, giving total leverage of 3.45x and net leverage of 3.29x, down from 4.75x and 4.50x at FY2025. That improvement is not clean. Q3 2026 contains a net construction recognition of 296 that the company itself says lifted Adjusted EBITDA, and LTM includes net construction recognitions of 218 across the twelve months. Removing them, LTM Adjusted EBITDA is 1,216 and net leverage is 3.88x, which is close to the management figure of approximately 3.9x (a management statement whose definition is not in the pack, so the match is an observation and not a reconciliation). Corporate debt rose by 343 in nine months, of which 360 is revolver drawn (130 to 490); unrestricted cash fell from 239 to 227 and undrawn revolver capacity from 809 to 457, so corporate liquidity is 684 against 1,048 at year end. Nine-month free cash flow (273) was below share repurchases (410). Maturities are small through 2027, and the largest block falls due after 2030; the revolver matures January 2030. The credit read is therefore one of leverage that is moderate on the reported basis and elevated on a recurring basis, with liquidity adequate but declining and no covenant evidence to test headroom. Non-recourse receivable debt of 2,923 is excluded from these ratios; its inclusion would put total debt at 7,869 and is shown for information only.

facts.text: Period and perimeter checks: every ratio uses period-end corporate debt (recourse) with a twelve-month earnings figure on the same consolidated perimeter. facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: HGV is a timeshare operator that sells vacation ownership interests, finances most of those sales through consumer loans, and manages the resorts and clubs under a long-term licence from Hilton. The business has two parts. Real estate sales and financing is cyclical and driven by tour flow and volume per guest; in Q3 2026 contract sales of 807 were down from 907 on a 12.5 percent lower volume per guest despite higher tour flow, and management cut full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance. Resort operations and club management is a cost-plus and fee business that is steadier but smaller than the real estate segment by segment Adjusted EBITDA. Financing converts sales into long-dated consumer receivables that are funded with non-recourse warehouse and securitisation debt, so the creditor reads two balance sheets in one filing: a recourse corporate stack and a receivable-backed non-recourse stack. The 2024 Bluegreen acquisition and 2021 Diamond acquisition expanded scale and are still being rebranded, which links future licence fees to rebranding milestones. In 2026 the company bought out the remainder of Elara for cash, upsized and added receivable facilities, refinanced a term loan to 2033 at unchanged pricing, repurchased stock beyond free cash flow and authorised a further repurchase plan. Ownership is public with a significant holder, Apollo, whose board and consent rights persist while it holds defined share thresholds. There is no sponsor-style dividend recapitalisation history in the sources and no dividends are planned. For the creditor, the transmission is: weaker sales conversion reduces Adjusted EBITDA and cash conversion; the corporate debt stack is covered by recurring fee income but with limited cushion if sales fall further; buyback appetite and acquisitions compete with deleveraging; and the legal permissions that govern distributions and additional debt cannot be read because the financing documents are not in the pack.

facts.text: Elara acquisition. On April 29, 2026 the company completed its acquisition of the remaining 75 percent of BRE Ace LLC, owner of the Elara timeshare resort, for total cash consideration of 131, taking it to 100 percent; the previously held 25 percent was an equity-method investment (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:8: "completed the acquisition of the remaining 75% ownership interest in BRE Ace LLC"). Status: completed, with preliminary purchase accounting that the company says could change materially (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:9: "Any potential adjustments made could be material in relation to the values presented in the table below."). The deal added timeshare financing receivables and non-recourse debt assumed; it was paid in cash; the sources do not state how the cash was funded, although the revolver drawn balance in the CP-1 base rose over the nine months (an observation, not a stated link). The Q1 report gave a price of 129 before closing adjustments; see Conflicts.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Non-recourse and receivable facilities. In May 2026 the Timeshare Facility was renewed and increased from 850 to 1.0 billion with maturity to May 2029 (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25: "increasing the facility size from $850 million to $1.0 billion"). On September 14, 2026 Big Cedar entered a 200 revolving receivables warehouse facility with 175 remaining capacity at September 30, 2026 (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25: "the Big Cedar Timeshare Facility has a remaining borrowing capacity of $175 million"). The NBA Receivables Facility was terminated in the third quarter (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:26: "During the third quarter of 2026, we terminated the NBA Receivables Facility."). Securitisations of approximately 500 of gross receivables in April 2026 and approximately 300 in June 2026 were completed with an advance rate of 98 percent, backed by pledged receivables and non-recourse to the corporate group (10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25: "The advance rate for this transaction was 98%."). These are receivable-funded; they do not add to the corporate debt figure but are the main refinancing channel for the non-recourse stack, and their availability depends on receivable performance and market access. The company states the proceeds were used to pay down debt and for general corporate purposes; that this supports corporate liquidity is an Analyst Interpretation.

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: Revenue durability. Evidence: management and club fees, financing revenue and servicing, plus rental revenue form the non-sales part of income (10-K_2025-12-31_hgv-20251231.htm.jsonl page:7: "Our management agreements with HOAs provide for a cost-plus management fee"), and a member base of 715,888. Credit implication: debt service coverage is better supported by the resort segment and financing margin than by sales, but the CP-1 corporate leverage of 3.88x net excluding net construction leaves limited tolerance for further sales declines. facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Hilton Grand Vacations is a leveraged but adequately liquid timeshare credit whose direction is weakening, so a cautious view is warranted. The strongest support is recurring income from resort management, club fees and loan servicing, a long-dated Hilton licence and corporate maturities that are small before 2028, with liquidity of USD 684 million. The weakest point is earnings quality: reported net leverage of 3.29x rises to 3.88x once net construction recognitions are removed, while third quarter sales conversion weakened and guidance was cut. What decides the outcome is whether sales conversion recovers enough to keep recurring leverage from rising, and whether the board favours debt reduction over buybacks of USD 410 million in nine months. Covenant headroom cannot be tested from the sources, which limits confidence to Medium.

facts.label: Assessment
facts.text: Thesis (Analyst Interpretation): recurring fee income and a back-ended corporate maturity profile support the debt, but the reliance on construction recognition in reported earnings, the thinner liquidity and the buyback pace leave less room for a further sales decline than reported leverage suggests.

citations.quote: Thesis (Analyst Interpretation): recurring fee income and a back-ended corporate maturity profile support the debt, but the reliance on construction recognition in reported earnings, the thinner liquidity and the buyback pace leave less room for a further sales decline than reported leverage suggests.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: First, the reported leverage understates the debt burden on recurring earnings. Hilton Grand Vacations has corporate debt of USD 4,946 million at September 30, 2026 against last twelve months Adjusted EBITDA of USD 1,434 million, giving total leverage of 3.45x and net leverage of 3.29x. That EBITDA includes net construction recognitions of USD 218 million; excluding them, EBITDA is USD 1,216 million and net leverage is 3.88x, close to the 3.9x management states on an undefined basis. The mechanism is timing: revenue and costs on units under construction are deferred and then recognised on completion, so a third quarter recognition of USD 296 million lifted reported earnings without new cash sales. For creditors this means leverage tolerance should be judged on the construction-adjusted figure, and the same adjustment changes interest cover from 5.07x to 4.30x.

For creditors this means leverage tolerance should be judged on the construction-adjusted figure, and the same adjustment changes interest cover from 5.07x to 4.30x.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Second, liquidity has thinned. Unrestricted cash of USD 227 million and undrawn revolver capacity of USD 457 million give corporate liquidity of USD 684 million, down from USD 1,048 million at December 31, 2025. The revolver drawn balance rose from USD 130 million to USD 490 million, and corporate debt rose by USD 343 million in nine months. Nine-month free cash flow of USD 273 million was below share repurchases of USD 410 million, and the revolver draw coincided with both the repurchases and the Elara purchase, though the sources do not state the draw's purpose. The implication is lower capacity to absorb a sales shortfall without further borrowing; the revolver matures in January 2030 and no facility expires within twelve months.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Third, sales conversion is the swing factor. Contract sales fell to USD 807 million in the third quarter from USD 907 million on a 12.5% lower volume per guest despite higher tour flow, and management reduced full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of USD 1.165 billion to USD 1.180 billion from USD 1.225 billion to USD 1.265 billion. Management attributes the shortfall to slow ramp of its execution initiatives; that is Management Language and is not adopted. The recurring resort and financing streams cushion the effect, but rental and ancillary services run at a loss and a larger owned-inventory mix needs more capital.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Fourth, the non-recourse stack and other claims sit beside the corporate debt. Non-recourse debt of USD 2,923 million is payable from pledged receivables and is excluded from the ratios; including it would put total borrowings at USD 7,869 million, a figure shown for information only. Further claims outside corporate debt include inventory purchase commitments of USD 304 million, marketing and licence commitments of USD 257 million and surety commitments of USD 346 million. The licence fee of 5% of gross revenues to Hilton is a fixed senior call on revenue. These claims reduce the cash available to the corporate creditor and make the receivable funding markets part of the credit risk.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. Recurring income is a genuine support (Documentary Fact): resort management fees are cost-plus, club fees follow the member base, and financing and servicing income comes from a receivable book that carries a double-digit weighted average interest rate, so these streams do not depend on new sales. The maturity profile is back-ended (Documentary Fact): corporate debt maturing is small until 2028 and the largest block falls due after 2030, which limits near-term refinancing need. Liquidity remains adequate (Documentary Fact): USD 684 million of cash and undrawn revolver capacity, with no corporate facility expiring within twelve months, plus separate non-recourse warehouse capacity that funds receivables. The Hilton licence is long dated (Documentary Fact): the initial term runs to 2116, protecting the brand that supports sales. Corporate interest cover on the reported basis is 5.07x and on the construction-adjusted basis 4.30x (Analyst Interpretation), which suggests debt service is covered by current earnings.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Weaknesses. Earnings quality is lower than reported (Analyst Interpretation): a third quarter construction recognition and an allowance estimate change raised reported results, and the allowance effect on Adjusted EBITDA is not separately stated. Sales conversion is weakening (Documentary Fact): contract sales declined on lower volume per guest and guidance was cut. Capital allocation competes with deleveraging (Documentary Fact): repurchases of USD 410 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 273 million in nine months, and a further USD 600 million plan was authorised. The Hilton licence is a fixed senior call (Documentary Fact): a fee of 5% of gross revenues and rebranding milestones that, if missed, add up to 1% to the fee. Visibility on creditor protections is absent (Insufficient Information): covenant levels, guarantor identities, collateral and permitted-payment terms are not in the sources, which matters because the Senior Notes due 2032 are secured and the others unsecured. The Elara acquisition accounting is preliminary and its price is logged differently in two filings (Documentary Fact), a minor source conflict that does not change the view.

facts.label: Evidence trace view
facts.text: Hilton Grand Vacations' analysis can be traced to its sources for the debt, liquidity, earnings and business facts it uses, but not for the legal protections a creditor would rely on. Every quotation in the three evidence-bearing handoffs sits on the page it cites, every ratio and total reproduces from the cited figures, and the credit synthesis uses only figures present in the financial base. The defects found are minor: wrong or surplus page references on a few rows, one loosely worded debt increase, a comparison of a nine month mix with a full year mix, and one strengths label that states an inference as fact. The weakest point is absence, not error: no covenant text, guarantor terms or ratings exist in the sources, so those conclusions are explicit gaps. The result is a traceable factual base with a bounded legal view.

spans.text: ## Request

Module: source readiness for Hilton Grand Vacations Inc. (ticker HGV, Commission file number 001-37794), as of 2026-11-05, evidence cutoff 2026-11-05. Pathway: credit snapshot. Reporting currency: USD, in millions unless a source states otherwise (context file). Current period: Q3 2026 (quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026); prior period: FY2025 (year ended December 31, 2025).

Question answered: can the supplied source set support the selected downstream work (CP-1 financial and debt extraction, CP-1A business and transaction context, CP-2 credit synthesis, CP-5 evidence trace review), and what remains blocked? This module gives no credit conclusion, no legal interpretation and no investment opinion, and it calculates nothing; it distinguishes source sufficiency from completion of downstream analysis. ## Findings

### Financial base view

On the reported basis, Hilton Grand Vacations carries corporate debt of 4,946 (gross) at September 30, 2026 against LTM Adjusted EBITDA of 1,434, giving total leverage of 3.45x and net leverage of 3.29x, down from 4.75x and 4.50x at FY2025. That improvement is not clean. Q3 2026 contains a net construction recognition of 296 that the company itself says lifted Adjusted EBITDA, and LTM includes net construction recognitions of 218 across the twelve months. Removing them, LTM Adjusted EBITDA is 1,216 and net leverage is 3.88x, which is close to the management figure of approximately 3.9x (a management statement whose definition is not in the pack, so the match is an observation and not a reconciliation). Corporate debt rose by 343 in nine months, of which 360 is revolver drawn (130 to 490); unrestricted cash fell from 239 to 227 and undrawn revolver capacity from 809 to 457, so corporate liquidity is 684 against 1,048 at year end. Nine-month free cash flow (273) was below share repurchases (410). Maturities are small through 2027, and the largest block falls due after 2030; the revolver matures January 2030. The credit read is therefore one of leverage that is moderate on the reported basis and elevated on a recurring basis, with liquidity adequate but declining and no covenant evidence to test headroom. Non-recourse receivable debt of 2,923 is excluded from these ratios; its inclusion would put total debt at 7,869 and is shown for information only.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Hilton Grand Vacations is a Hilton-licensed timeshare operator with recurring management and financing income alongside a cyclical, sales-driven real estate segment. Third quarter sales weakened, guidance was cut, and acquisitions plus buybacks drive capital allocation. | Medium | No ratings, no executed financing or sponsor documents, and no investor presentation are in the sources. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Contract sales fell in the third quarter on lower volume per guest, and full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance was reduced. | Weaker sales conversion pressures earnings and leverage, as reported results were lifted by a construction recognition. | High |

| Resort management, club fees and loan servicing provide recurring income that does not depend on new sales. | These streams support debt service when sales weaken, though rental and ancillary services run at a loss. | Medium |
| The Hilton licence is long dated but carries a fee of 5% of gross revenues and rebranding milestones. | The fee is a fixed senior call on revenue, and missed milestones raise it. | High |

| Apollo retains board and consent rights through a stockholders agreement and has been selling shares. | A concentrated holder can influence control events; its current holding after the June 2026 offering is not disclosed. | Medium |

| Capital allocation favours buybacks and acquisitions: Elara was bought for cash and repurchases exceeded free cash flow in nine months. | Shareholder returns compete with deleveraging; no dividend is paid. | Medium |
### Business and transaction view

HGV is a timeshare operator that sells vacation ownership interests, finances most of those sales through consumer loans, and manages the resorts and clubs under a long-term licence from Hilton. The business has two parts. Real estate sales and financing is cyclical and driven by tour flow and volume per guest; in Q3 2026 contract sales of 807 were down from 907 on a 12.5 percent lower volume per guest despite higher tour flow, and management cut full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance. Resort operations and club management is a cost-plus and fee business that is steadier but smaller than the real estate segment by segment Adjusted EBITDA. Financing converts sales into long-dated consumer receivables that are funded with non-recourse warehouse and securitisation debt, so the creditor reads two balance sheets in one filing: a recourse corporate stack and a receivable-backed non-recourse stack. The 2024 Bluegreen acquisition and 2021 Diamond acquisition expanded scale and are still being rebranded, which links future licence fees to rebranding milestones. In 2026 the company bought out the remainder of Elara for cash, upsized and added receivable facilities, refinanced a term loan to 2033 at unchanged pricing, repurchased stock beyond free cash flow and authorised a further repurchase plan. Ownership is public with a significant holder, Apollo, whose board and consent rights persist while it holds defined share thresholds. There is no sponsor-style dividend recapitalisation history in the sources and no dividends are planned. For the creditor, the transmission is: weaker sales conversion reduces Adjusted EBITDA and cash conversion; the corporate debt stack is covered by recurring fee income but with limited cushion if sales fall further; buyback appetite and acquisitions compete with deleveraging; and the legal permissions that govern distributions and additional debt cannot be read because the financing documents are not in the pack.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No leveraged buyout, sponsor transaction or new bond issue occurs in the sources. The financing and corporate events in the period are as follows, each with its status and the CP-1 link where one exists.

Elara acquisition. On April 29, 2026 the company completed its acquisition of the remaining 75 percent of BRE Ace LLC, owner of the Elara timeshare resort, for total cash consideration of 131, taking it to 100 percent; the previously held 25 percent was an equity-method investment (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:8`: "completed the acquisition of the remaining 75% ownership interest in BRE Ace LLC"). Status: completed, with preliminary purchase accounting that the company says could change materially (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:9`: "Any potential adjustments made could be material in relation to the values presented in the table below."). The deal added timeshare financing receivables and non-recourse debt assumed; it was paid in cash; the sources do not state how the cash was funded, although the revolver drawn balance in the CP-1 base rose over the nine months (an observation, not a stated link). The Q1 report gave a price of 129 before closing adjustments; see Conflicts.

Corporate debt events. On July 17, 2026 the company refinanced its Term Loan B due 2028 with an amended 850 Term Loan B due 2033 at unchanged pricing of SOFR plus 2.00 percent (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:23`). Status: completed, a subsequent event in the Q2 report (`10-Q_2026-06-30_hgv-20260630.htm.jsonl page:24`: "On July 17, 2026, we refinanced our Term Loan B due 2028 with an amended $850 million Term Loan B due 2033."). Liquidity effect: moves that term loan maturity from 2028 to 2033; the CP-1 maturity profile shows corporate debt maturing before 2028 as small. Use of proceeds: refinancing; no new debt amount was raised beyond the refinanced balance (the sources do not state any fees or net new money).

Non-recourse and receivable facilities. In May 2026 the Timeshare Facility was renewed and increased from 850 to 1.0 billion with maturity to May 2029 (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25`: "increasing the facility size from $850 million to $1.0 billion"). On September 14, 2026 Big Cedar entered a 200 revolving receivables warehouse facility with 175 remaining capacity at September 30, 2026 (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25`: "the Big Cedar Timeshare Facility has a remaining borrowing capacity of $175 million"). The NBA Receivables Facility was terminated in the third quarter (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:26`: "During the third quarter of 2026, we terminated the NBA Receivables Facility."). Securitisations of approximately 500 of gross receivables in April 2026 and approximately 300 in June 2026 were completed with an advance rate of 98 percent, backed by pledged receivables and non-recourse to the corporate group (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:25`: "The advance rate for this transaction was 98%."). These are receivable-funded; they do not add to the corporate debt figure but are the main refinancing channel for the non-recourse stack, and their availability depends on receivable performance and market access. The company states the proceeds were used to pay down debt and for general corporate purposes; that this supports corporate liquidity is an Analyst Interpretation.

Equity and capital returns. The company repurchased 9 million shares for 410 in nine months 2026, and on August 12, 2026 the board authorised a further 600 plan that starts when the earlier plan is complete (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:59`). In June 2026 the company repurchased 750,000 shares for 38 from the underwriters in a secondary offering by Apollo-managed entities at 50.00 per share (`10-Q_2026-09-30_hgv-20260930.htm.jsonl page:31`: "for an aggregate purchase price of $38 million (or $50.00 per share)"). Status: completed. Effect: cash returned to shareholders ahead of debt reduction.

Subsequent events after September 30, 2026: none beyond the October 29, 2026 release; the release reduced FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance (excluding deferrals and recognitions) to 1.165 to 1.180 billion from 1.225 to 1.265 billion, a Management Language statement (`EX-99.1_2026-10-29_hgvq32026earningsreleaseex.htm.jsonl page:2`). No Q4 2026 information is in the pack.
### Ownership, control and governance
| Topic | Fact | Category | Locator | Quote | Mechanic |

| Ownership class | Public company; Hilton retained no ownership after the 2017 spin-off | Documentary Fact | `10-K_2025-12-31_hgv-20251231.htm.jsonl page:5` | "Following the spin-off, Hilton did not retain any" | No sponsor; Hilton relationship is contractual, through the licence |

| Apollo stake | Apollo Investors owned 18,245,825 Apollo Closing Shares at February 19, 2026 | Documentary Fact | `10-K_2025-12-31_hgv-20251231.htm.jsonl page:27` | "As of February 19, 2026, the Apollo Investors owned an aggregate of 18,245,825 Apollo Closing Shares." | Largest identified holder; percentage not computed because the share count at that date is not read |

spans.text: ## Request

Fundamental credit synthesis for Hilton Grand Vacations Inc., as of 2026-11-05, credit snapshot pathway. Scope: the creditor view of the consolidated corporate (recourse) debt, built only from the accepted source readiness, financial base and business context handoffs, with USD as the reporting currency and Q3 2026 and FY2025 as the periods.
## Sources
### Issuer sources relied on (through the upstream handoffs; this module quotes no source text)
| Source (exact name) | sha256 |
| EX-99.1_2026-04-30_hgvq12026earningsreleaseex.htm.jsonl | 92e4f803974e8b1d1fb782b7fa4c071295d1bcd965fc060f8d1edf8b3dca9f05 |
| EX-99.1_2026-07-30_hgvq22026earningsreleaseex.htm.jsonl | 5535f4d3e680b0dd2b2a79102a2a9c458f84caa70b4ad3b4d26b8a0600e150b0 |
Run context sha256 6edd9e91feb582497e031062a9d2821be0472a4f8a6020100729ec6b65f6bb35 (settings, not evidence).
### Handoffs supplied
| Module | sha256 | Use |
| CP-0 | 7f439ceea4fa01d10d2964db467b9c8db2afe1ab216f19ad970291bc172cd742 | Source readiness and inherited limitations |
| CP-1 | 1deb6dff00cc26d7b003e387964ad65a7dd8c1a085dac876c08152976dc6e037 | Financial base: leverage, cover, liquidity, maturities, claims outside corporate debt |
| CP-1A | aedd714085709d5f0b1d5b25264c9dd9d006337bf5d12d570e12a229e724c81b | Business model, ownership, governance, transactions and the logged Elara price conflict |
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Hilton Grand Vacations is a cautious credit: leverage looks moderate on reported earnings but high on recurring earnings, liquidity is adequate but falling, sales weakened in the third quarter, and buybacks compete with debt reduction. | Medium | Covenant terms, financing documents and ratings are not in the sources, so headroom and legal protections cannot be tested. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |
| Reported leverage of 3.29x net falls to 3.88x net excluding net construction recognitions. | The recurring-earnings figure is the safer basis for judging debt capacity. | Medium |
| Liquidity was USD 684 million at September 30, 2026, against USD 1,048 million at year end. | Cushion for a sales downturn is thinner, and the revolver is more drawn. | High |
| Nine-month free cash flow of USD 273 million was below share repurchases of USD 410 million. | Shareholder returns are slowing deleveraging. | Medium |
| Corporate maturities are small before 2028, with most debt due after 2030. | Refinancing pressure is limited in the near term. | High |

| Recurring management, club and servicing income supports debt service, but third quarter sales conversion weakened and guidance was cut. | Earnings are more exposed to sales than the recurring base suggests. | Medium |
### Credit view

Hilton Grand Vacations is a leveraged but adequately liquid timeshare credit whose direction is weakening, so a cautious view is warranted. The strongest support is recurring income from resort management, club fees and loan servicing, a long-dated Hilton licence and corporate maturities that are small before 2028, with liquidity of USD 684 million. The weakest point is earnings quality: reported net leverage of 3.29x rises to 3.88x once net construction recognitions are removed, while third quarter sales conversion weakened and guidance was cut. What decides the outcome is whether sales conversion recovers enough to keep recurring leverage from rising, and whether the board favours debt reduction over buybacks of USD 410 million in nine months. Covenant headroom cannot be tested from the sources, which limits confidence to Medium.
### Assessment

Category: Analyst Interpretation. Confidence: Medium. Basis: financial base figures (reported and construction-adjusted leverage, liquidity, free cash flow against repurchases, maturity profile) and the business context rows on contract sales, recurring fee streams, licence terms and capital allocation. The view is Medium and not High because the business context handoff judged this module ready only with limitations, and the covenant package is Not supplied.

Thesis (Analyst Interpretation): recurring fee income and a back-ended corporate maturity profile support the debt, but the reliance on construction recognition in reported earnings, the thinner liquidity and the buyback pace leave less room for a further sales decline than reported leverage suggests.
### Key findings

First, the reported leverage understates the debt burden on recurring earnings. Hilton Grand Vacations has corporate debt of USD 4,946 million at September 30, 2026 against last twelve months Adjusted EBITDA of USD 1,434 million, giving total leverage of 3.45x and net leverage of 3.29x. That EBITDA includes net construction recognitions of USD 218 million; excluding them, EBITDA is USD 1,216 million and net leverage is 3.88x, close to the 3.9x management states on an undefined basis. The mechanism is timing: revenue and costs on units under construction are deferred and then recognised on completion, so a third quarter recognition of USD 296 million lifted reported earnings without new cash sales. For creditors this means leverage tolerance should be judged on the construction-adjusted figure, and the same adjustment changes interest cover from 5.07x to 4.30x.

Second, liquidity has thinned. Unrestricted cash of USD 227 million and undrawn revolver capacity of USD 457 million give corporate liquidity of USD 684 million, down from USD 1,048 million at December 31, 2025. The revolver drawn balance rose from USD 130 million to USD 490 million, and corporate debt rose by USD 343 million in nine months. Nine-month free cash flow of USD 273 million was below share repurchases of USD 410 million, and the revolver draw coincided with both the repurchases and the Elara purchase, though the sources do not state the draw's purpose. The implication is lower capacity to absorb a sales shortfall without further borrowing; the revolver matures in January 2030 and no facility expires within twelve months.

Third, sales conversion is the swing factor. Contract sales fell to USD 807 million in the third quarter from USD 907 million on a 12.5% lower volume per guest despite higher tour flow, and management reduced full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of USD 1.165 billion to USD 1.180 billion from USD 1.225 billion to USD 1.265 billion. Management attributes the shortfall to slow ramp of its execution initiatives; that is Management Language and is not adopted. The recurring resort and financing streams cushion the effect, but rental and ancillary services run at a loss and a larger owned-inventory mix needs more capital.

Fourth, the non-recourse stack and other claims sit beside the corporate debt. Non-recourse debt of USD 2,923 million is payable from pledged receivables and is excluded from the ratios; including it would put total borrowings at USD 7,869 million, a figure shown for information only. Further claims outside corporate debt include inventory purchase commitments of USD 304 million, marketing and licence commitments of USD 257 million and surety commitments of USD 346 million. The licence fee of 5% of gross revenues to Hilton is a fixed senior call on revenue. These claims reduce the cash available to the corporate creditor and make the receivable funding markets part of the credit risk.

Fifth, control and capital allocation are board-driven. Apollo retains board and consent rights while above share thresholds and has been selling stock, with its holding after the June 2026 offering not disclosed. No dividend is planned, and the company repurchased shares alongside the offering. Governance behaviour is documented as Neutral or Mixed: no priming, drop-down or extraction is evidenced, but legal capacity under the credit agreement and indentures is Not supplied, so what the documents permit cannot be assessed.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. Recurring income is a genuine support (Documentary Fact): resort management fees are cost-plus, club fees follow the member base, and financing and servicing income comes from a receivable book that carries a double-digit weighted average interest rate, so these streams do not depend on new sales. The maturity profile is back-ended (Documentary Fact): corporate debt maturing is small until 2028 and the largest block falls due after 2030, which limits near-term refinancing need. Liquidity remains adequate (Documentary Fact): USD 684 million of cash and undrawn revolver capacity, with no corporate facility expiring within twelve months, plus separate non-recourse warehouse capacity that funds receivables. The Hilton licence is long dated (Documentary Fact): the initial term runs to 2116, protecting the brand that supports sales. Corporate interest cover on the reported basis is 5.07x and on the construction-adjusted basis 4.30x (Analyst Interpretation), which suggests debt service is covered by current earnings.

Weaknesses. Earnings quality is lower than reported (Analyst Interpretation): a third quarter construction recognition and an allowance estimate change raised reported results, and the allowance effect on Adjusted EBITDA is not separately stated. Sales conversion is weakening (Documentary Fact): contract sales declined on lower volume per guest and guidance was cut. Capital allocation competes with deleveraging (Documentary Fact): repurchases of USD 410 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 273 million in nine months, and a further USD 600 million plan was authorised. The Hilton licence is a fixed senior call (Documentary Fact): a fee of 5% of gross revenues and rebranding milestones that, if missed, add up to 1% to the fee. Visibility on creditor protections is absent (Insufficient Information): covenant levels, guarantor identities, collateral and permitted-payment terms are not in the sources, which matters because the Senior Notes due 2032 are secured and the others unsecured. The Elara acquisition accounting is preliminary and its price is logged differently in two filings (Documentary Fact), a minor source conflict that does not change the view.
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Sales conversion keeps declining | Lower volume per guest cuts contract sales, owned-inventory margin and cash conversion, while the fixed licence fee and sales costs stay | Recurring leverage rises above 3.88x net and cover falls toward 4.30x, against covenant tests whose levels are Not supplied | Material |

| Reported earnings flatter leverage | Construction recognitions and the allowance change raised Q3 results; a reversal or completion of recognition lowers reported EBITDA | Reported leverage of 3.29x is not a reliable guide; use the construction-adjusted figure | Material |

| Liquidity erosion through buybacks and acquisitions | Revolver drawn balance rose while repurchases exceeded free cash flow | Liquidity of USD 684 million could fall further and the revolver is the only committed corporate source | Material |

| Receivable funding access | The non-recourse stack of USD 2,923 million depends on securitisation and warehouse markets and receivable performance | A shock to receivable performance could restrict funding and raise corporate support needs | Material |
| Unknown legal protections | Credit agreement, indentures and guarantor terms are not in the sources | Debt incurrence, restricted payments and priming capacity cannot be assessed | Material |
| Control event | Apollo's board and consent rights and its continuing sales of stock | Possible shift in ownership and strategy; effect on creditors is not determinable from the sources | Minor |
## Calculations

No new calculation is made in this module. Every figure is a reference to the accepted financial base: corporate debt USD 4,946 million; last twelve months Adjusted EBITDA USD 1,434 million; net construction recognitions USD 218 million; Adjusted EBITDA excluding them USD 1,216 million; total leverage 3.45x; net leverage 3.29x and 3.88x excluding net construction; interest cover 5.07x and 4.30x excluding net construction; liquidity USD 684 million against USD 1,048 million; revolver drawn USD 490 million against USD 130 million; corporate debt increase USD 343 million; nine-month free cash flow USD 273 million; repurchases USD 410 million; non-recourse debt USD 2,923 million; total borrowings USD 7,869 million (information only). The statement that net leverage excluding net construction is close to the 3.9x management figure is an observation, not a reconciliation, because the management definition is Not supplied.

| Covenant test levels, definitions and headroom are Not supplied; only a general compliance statement exists | Headroom for the leverage and financial ratio tests cannot be assessed | Financial risk, default risk | High | Add the credit agreement, amendments and compliance certificate |

| Indentures, guarantor identities, collateral and permitted-payment terms are Not supplied | Legal capacity for distributions, debt and priming cannot be read | Creditor control, loss given default | High | Add the executed financing documents |

| Management leverage of about 3.9x has no definition in the sources | Cannot be reconciled to analyst figures | Leverage comparison | Medium | Treat as a management claim |
| Elara purchase accounting is preliminary and the price is logged differently in two filings | Acquired balances may change | Receivables and non-recourse debt | Low | Re-check at the next filing |

| No pro forma earnings for Elara in the last twelve months and no information after October 29, 2026 | Leverage may differ on a pro forma or later basis | Leverage | Low | Update at the fourth quarter filing |

Proceed to CP-5 (evidence trace review). It should test the construction-adjusted leverage and liquidity figures against the financial base, confirm that every Management Language row stays labelled, and check that the Elara price conflict is carried as logged and not reconciled.
